mcqs.question: A screen has ten independent widgets, each reading its own small piece of state, versus a version where all ten read one shared top-level state object. Why does the second version recompose more?
options: Shared state objects always cause every composable in the app to recompose, not just the screen

Compose can only prove it's safe to skip a composable if it can isolate exactly what changed; when all ten read one shared object, any change to any part of it looks like a change to everything they read, so all ten recompose
The number of widgets alone determines recomposition scope, regardless of what state they read
Recomposition scope is fixed at compile time and cannot depend on runtime state structure
mcqs.explanation: Smart recomposition skips composables that don't read the specific state that changed — when many composables all read one shared object, a change anywhere in it is indistinguishable from a change relevant to all of them, so none can be safely skipped, unlike widgets each reading their own independent piece of state.

mcqs.question: A text field composable manages its own internal mutableStateOf for its text value, with no way for a caller to observe or control it. What's the fix to make it reusable?
options: Wrap it in a DisposableEffect
Add a rememberSaveable call inside it
Convert it to take value and onValueChange as parameters, moving state ownership up to the caller — state hoisting
Nothing needs to change; internal state is the correct default for reusable composables
mcqs.explanation: State hoisting moves ownership of the state to the nearest caller that needs to coordinate it, turning the composable into a stateless function of value and onValueChange — this is what makes it reusable and testable independent of where its state actually comes from.

mcqs.question: A composable uses plain remember to hold a search field's current text. What happens to that text when the device rotates?
options: It's cleared, because remember alone doesn't survive the composable being torn down and rebuilt by a configuration change — rememberSaveable would be needed to survive that
It survives rotation but not process death
It survives both rotation and process death automatically
remember and rememberSaveable behave identically in all cases
mcqs.explanation: Plain remember only survives recomposition within the same composition instance, not the composable being destroyed and recreated by a configuration change like rotation — rememberSaveable layers Bundle-based save/restore on top specifically to survive that, and process death for small enough data.

mcqs.question: A composable needs to subscribe to a callback-based location API and must unsubscribe when it leaves composition. Which side-effect API is designed for this?
options: remember
DisposableEffect, because it provides an onDispose block Compose guarantees to call on cleanup
A plain var declared in the composable body
State hoisting
mcqs.explanation: DisposableEffect exists specifically for effects needing explicit cleanup like unsubscribing from a callback API, guaranteeing the onDispose block runs when the composable leaves composition or its key changes — LaunchedEffect handles coroutines but has no equivalent cleanup contract for callback-based subscriptions.

mcqs.question: A composable reads a plain Kotlin var that's mutated elsewhere in the code, but the UI never updates when the value changes. Why?
options: Compose only reacts to reads of observable state through the State snapshot system; a plain var gives it nothing to subscribe to, so mutating it produces no recomposition regardless of the value actually changing
The var must be declared as private to work with Compose
Compose has a bug that requires a manual invalidate() call
Plain vars are automatically converted to observable state at compile time, so this shouldn't be possible
mcqs.explanation: Recomposition is driven entirely by reads of observable state (mutableStateOf, StateFlow via collectAsState, etc.) — a bare var participates in none of that tracking, so Compose has no way to know it changed and never re-runs the composable, regardless of how correctly the mutation itself executes.

mcqs.question: A composable feels sluggish specifically while the user types in a search field, but renders fine on first load. What's the most likely cause?
options: An expensive computation (like filtering a large list) running directly in the composable's body with no memoization, re-executing on every recomposition triggered by each keystroke
The device's CPU throttling due to the search field being open too long
A memory leak in the TextField composable itself
The search field should be converted to a DisposableEffect
mcqs.explanation: Because a composable body runs on every recomposition, not once, unmemoized expensive work re-executes on every keystroke that triggers a recompose — remember (with the right keys) caches the result so it only recomputes when something relevant actually changes, which is the standard fix for exactly this symptom.
